new.n: The Old Silver Mine: Bill Pond's 1870s shaft across from Porter's Mills
new.pl: Base of the sandstone ridge on the west bank of the Chippewa, along Silver Mine Drive, across the river from Porter's Mills
new.v: Coins and picnic losses from the grove years; the pit itself
new.st: In the 1870s a clairvoyant's spirit guide 'Big Heart' pointed to a spot 'four miles south of the city', and logging contractor Bill Pond 'dug a shaft or pit down through the soil and into the sandstone rock'. Gard: 'This place, still known as the Old Silver Mine, is located at the base of a sandstone ridge across the Chippewa River from the once thriving lumbering settlement of Porters Mills.' It was later a favorite Eau Claire picnic ground in an oak grove. The 1972 USGS Eau Claire West topo names the road at the foot of that ridge Silver Mine Drive (sec. 34 T27N R10W), which fixes the stretch; the pin is on the drive opposite Porter's Mills. The 2020 LiDAR shows a small square-cut notch in the slope about 50 m north of the pin, a candidate for the old pit; good to about 400 m along the drive.
new.t: No silver here: the coins to look for are from the picnic-grove years, in the oak grove along the ridge foot. Check the notch 50 m north of the pin first. Private land along the drive: ask.
src: Gard, Wisconsin Lore (1962), ch. 8 Buried Treasure Tales (PC on-screen read of borrowed copy)
USGS Eau Claire West 1:24,000 topo (1972): Silver Mine Drive
new.pinev: Base of the sandstone ridge on the west bank of the Chippewa, along Silver Mine Drive, across the river from Porter's Mills

new.n: Stevenson Creek chimney and lumber camp, Trout Lake (about 1905-1911)
new.pl: Mouth of Stevenson Creek on Trout Lake (NHDPlus), by Hwy M
new.st: A big three-story stone chimney stands on the north shore of Stevenson Creek where it feeds Trout Lake: Arthur L. Stevenson's home, about 1905-1911. Across the creek was a lumber camp with a sawmill and a railroad spur: 'the big lumber mill across the creek lay where the North Trout Lake nature trail is today just west of Highway M'. Barracks were in use in 1910, and a rotted bunkhouse was still seen in 1936 (Hollatz 2000). Pin: the creek mouth as NHDPlus draws it.
new.t: State forest land (Northern Highland-American Legion): the chimney is a ruin to look at; ask the DNR before detecting the camp side.

new.n: Schutzen Park: German shooting-club park and dance hall (about 1885-1899)
new.pl: 20 acres about 1.5 blocks from the Second Ward school (Main St east of McGraw St, 1897 Sanborn sheet 10), Eau Claire
new.v: Coins, tokens, lead bullets and shot, beer-garden finds
new.st: Schutzen Park was the German sharpshooters' park, with a shooting range and a dance hall. The Germania Singing Society held galas there, and it hosted Fourth of July crowds (Eau Claire Leader, 5 Jul 1896, p. 5; about 254 Leader hits 1885-1899). In November 1899 it was offered for sale as "20 acres of city property one and a half blocks from the Second Ward school house, known as the Schutzen Park" (Eau Claire Leader, 2 Nov 1899, p. 2). The 1897 Sanborn map shows the Second Ward No. 1 public school on Main Street, east of McGraw Street (sheet 10). The pin is on that school block (Main St just east of McGraw St, from today's parcel addresses); the 20-acre park lay within about 1.5 blocks, so it is good to about 400 m until the tract is found on the 1897 Sanborn edges or the 1902 county map.
new.t: Shooting parks leave lead shot and bullets behind the targets and coins around the dance hall and tables. Twenty open acres in 1899 should show as an unbuilt tract on the 1897 Sanborn edges or the 1902 county map. Most of it is likely house lots now, so look for park or school lawns that survive.
src: Eau Claire Leader, 2 Nov 1899, p. 2 (newspapers.com image 239428945)
